trivia: Did you know that Morse code is still widely used today? It might be why we are making you do this.
Morse code was designed so the most common letters are the shortest. E is a single dot. Samuel Morse counted the letters in a printer's type case to work that out.
SOS was chosen as the distress signal because it is easy to key and hard to mistake: three dots, three dashes, three dots. It does not stand for anything.
Pilots still identify radio beacons by Morse. Some aircraft cockpits play it to them, whether they like it or not.
The last commercial Morse message in the United States was sent in nineteen ninety-nine. It read: what hath God wrought. The same as the very first one.
A trained operator can send around forty words a minute. You are doing fine. Probably.
Morse code is not a binary code. Dots, dashes and three lengths of silence. It is closer to a five symbol alphabet.
Amateur radio operators still hold Morse contests. The record for receiving is over seventy words a minute. Nobody at this stall is expected to match it.
Before Morse, long distance messages moved at the speed of a horse. After it, at the speed of light down a wire. That is quite the upgrade.
The space bar you are hammering has one job today. Please be gentle with it. It has a long afternoon ahead.
In the film Interstellar, the whole plot turns on Morse code sent through a wristwatch. Do not try that with the laptops.
Blink patterns in Morse have been used by prisoners of war to send messages on camera. Yours only needs to reach the projector.

human-or-ai.trivia: The human texts here are real office emails from before two thousand and two. Nobody had a chat bot to write them. They had coffee.
Language models are trained to produce the most likely next word. Humans are trained by deadlines. That is usually the tell.
People make typos, skip greetings and trail off. Models balance their clauses and sign off politely. Unless they are told not to.
